intro: Nigeria is Africa's most populous country, with about 238 million people (2025). Most of the money it earns from selling abroad comes from oil, yet many of its people are still poor. This lesson is a case study of one NEE. It covers where Nigeria is and why it matters, and how its economy is changing. It also covers what big foreign companies bring, and how development changes people's lives and the environment.

basics.text: Nigeria is a country in West Africa. Africa is a continent: a huge area of land with many countries.
Population is the number of people living in a place.
A country's economy is all the work, buying and selling that happens there. It includes farms, factories, shops and offices.
Trade is buying and selling between countries. Selling goods to another country is exporting. Buying goods from another country is importing.
A company is a business that sells goods or services. Profit is the money left over after it has paid all its costs.
Investment means putting money into something, such as a new factory. The aim is to get more back later.
Pollution is harmful stuff getting into the air, water or land. Oil spilled into a river is pollution.

keyPoints.heading: Nigeria in context
keyPoints.content: Nigeria is in West Africa, on the coast of the Gulf of Guinea. It has about 238 million people (2025), more than any other African country, and an economy worth about $291 billion a year. It is an NEE: a newly emerging economy, growing as it builds up industry and services. Regionally, in West Africa, Nigeria is the biggest economy. It is the biggest member of ECOWAS. This group of West African countries works to make trade between them easier. Globally, it is a major oil exporter, and its films and music are watched and heard around the world. Its wider context matters too. Politically, Britain ruled Nigeria until independence, and since then there have been military governments as well as elected ones. Socially and culturally, Nigeria has hundreds of ethnic groups. The largest are the Hausa-Fulani in the north and the Yoruba and Igbo in the south. Most people in the north are Muslim and most in the south are Christian. Environmentally, it has dry grassland in the north and rainforest, mangroves and the oil-rich Niger Delta in the south.

keyTerms.def: Newly emerging economy: a country whose economy has started to grow fast as it builds up industry, such as Nigeria, India or Brazil.
The Economic Community of West African States: a group of West African countries working to make trade between them easier. Nigeria is its largest member.
The large wetland area in southern Nigeria where the River Niger reaches the sea. Most of Nigeria's oil comes from here.
How important a country is within its own part of the world: for Nigeria, within West Africa.

keyPoints.memTip: Regional = West Africa; global = the whole world.
keyPoints.tutor_note: "Regionally important" means within its world region, West Africa, not within Nigeria.

keyPoints.heading: Nigeria's changing economy
keyPoints.content: An economy has sectors. The primary sector takes raw materials from the land or sea: farming, fishing, oil. The secondary sector makes things in factories: manufacturing. The tertiary sector provides services such as shops, banks, health care and films. Nigeria's economy used to depend on farming. Then oil was found in the Niger Delta. Today fuel (oil and gas) makes up about 86% of the goods Nigeria sells abroad. But oil gives jobs to few people, because machines do most of the work. When the world oil price falls, Nigeria's income falls with it. In 2025 services made up about 58% of Nigeria's economy, industry about 16% and farming about 23%. Farming still gave about a third of all jobs. So most of the economy is now services, even though oil and gas earn most of the export money. Factories in and around Lagos, Nigeria's biggest city, make food, drinks, cement and soap. Services such as banking, mobile phones and Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, are growing fast. Manufacturing can stimulate development. Factory jobs pay regular wages. Workers spend their wages in local shops, which then need more staff. The government collects more tax to spend on schools and roads. One new factory can lead to many more jobs in this way. This is called the multiplier effect.
writeBullets: Sectors: primary (raw materials), secondary (manufacturing), tertiary (services)
Fuel is about 86% of Nigeria's goods exports (2025), but oil gives few jobs
Balance (2025): services about 58% of the economy, industry 16%, farming 23%; farming still about a third of jobs
Falling oil prices cut Nigeria's income: a reason to diversify
Growth of manufacturing (Lagos: food, drinks, cement, soap) and services (banking, phones, Nollywood)
Manufacturing stimulates development: wages, spending, more jobs, more tax: the multiplier effect

keyTerms.def: Jobs that take raw materials from the land or sea, such as farming, fishing, mining and oil.
Jobs that make things, such as factory work. Also called manufacturing.
Jobs that provide a service, such as shops, banks, health care, teaching and films.
When one new business leads to more jobs and spending elsewhere, as workers spend their wages and the government collects more tax.
Nigeria's film industry, based mainly in Lagos: an example of the economy growing beyond oil.

keyPoints.memTip: Oil earns the money but makes few jobs; factories and services spread jobs further.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Explain the chain from a factory to development step by step: wages, spending, more jobs, taxes.

keyPoints.heading: TNCs in Nigeria: Shell and Unilever
keyPoints.content: A TNC (transnational corporation) is a company that works in many countries. Its headquarters are usually in a rich country. Shell, an oil company based in the UK, took oil from the Niger Delta on land for decades. In 2025 it sold that business to a Nigerian-owned company, but it still produces oil from deep water off the coast. Unilever makes soap, food and drinks in factories in Nigeria. Advantages for Nigeria: TNCs give jobs and train local workers in new skills. They pay taxes, and oil companies also pay the government for the oil they take. They build roads and other facilities, and bring new technology. Unilever buys from Nigerian suppliers, which creates more local jobs. Disadvantages: much of the profit goes back to the TNC's home country instead of staying in Nigeria. Oil gives few jobs for the money it makes. Oil spills from pipelines have polluted creeks, farmland and fishing grounds in the Niger Delta. Some came from leaks and some from theft. Burning off spare gas pollutes the air. Local people have protested that they get the pollution but little of the money.

keyTerms.def: Transnational corporation: a company that works in more than one country, usually with its headquarters in a rich country.
When a foreign company sends its profits back to its home country instead of spending them where they were earned.
Burning off the gas that comes up with oil instead of using it. It wastes fuel and pollutes the air.

keyPoints.memTip: Shell drills: jobs and taxes in, profits and pollution out.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Explain how each advantage helps development, not just that it does: taxes pay for schools and clinics.

keyPoints.heading: Trade and aid
keyPoints.content: Nigeria's links with the rest of the world are changing. Trade: it sells mostly oil and gas, and buys machines, vehicles and food. It used to trade mostly with Europe and the USA; now China and India are big partners too. China has also lent money and built roads and railways, though some worry this leaves Nigeria in debt. Within West Africa, ECOWAS makes trade between member countries easier. Political relationships have changed too. Nigeria is a member of the Commonwealth. It was suspended while under military rule, and welcomed back once elected government returned. It is a leading member of the African Union and of ECOWAS. It has sent peacekeeping troops to other West African countries. Aid is help from other countries or charities: gifts, or loans on very easy terms. It comes in different types. Bilateral aid goes from one government to another, such as the UK's help for girls' schooling and health. Multilateral aid comes through international organisations, such as the World Bank or the United Nations. Charities, called NGOs (non-governmental organisations), run smaller projects, such as mosquito nets against malaria. Aid can save lives and pay for schools, clinics and clean water. But it can be wasted or stolen through corruption, and it may not reach the poorest people.
writeBullets: Exports mostly oil and gas; imports machines, vehicles, food
Trade shifting from Europe and the USA towards China and India
China: loans, roads and railways; worries about debt
ECOWAS: easier trade within West Africa
Political links: Commonwealth member (suspended under military rule, then back); leading in the African Union and ECOWAS; peacekeeping
Aid types: bilateral (government to government), multilateral (World Bank, UN), NGOs (charities)
Aid impacts: schools, clinics, mosquito nets; but corruption and waste

keyTerms.def: Aid given by one country's government directly to another's.
Aid given through international organisations such as the World Bank or the United Nations.
Non-governmental organisation: a charity, such as Oxfam, that runs aid projects.

keyPoints.memTip: Bi = two governments; multi = many, through an international body.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Aid is help on easy terms: gifts or very cheap loans. Do not confuse it with TNCs, tourism or commercial investment.

keyPoints.heading: Environmental impacts and quality of life
keyPoints.content: Economic development has costs for the environment. Oil spills poison creeks and kill fish and crops in the Niger Delta. In the Ogoni area of the delta, local people led by the writer Ken Saro-Wiwa protested against the pollution. He was executed by the military government of the time. Factories and traffic pollute the air of Lagos, and forests are cut down for farming and building. Development has also changed quality of life. Life expectancy rose from 47 years in 2000 to 55 in 2024, and infant mortality fell from 95 to 70 babies in every 1,000. More people have mobile phones and work in services. But the gains are uneven. The south, with the oil and Lagos, is richer. The north has more poverty, fewer children in school and has suffered attacks by the armed group Boko Haram. Nigeria's GNI per head is still only $1,360, so many people remain poor.

Ogoni protests led by Ken Saro-Wiwa, executed by the military government

Uneven: richer south, poorer north (fewer in school, Boko Haram attacks)

keyTerms.def: A Nigerian writer who led peaceful protests by the Ogoni people against oil pollution. He was executed by Nigeria's military government.
An armed extremist group in north-east Nigeria whose attacks have forced many people from their homes.
How good people's lives are: their health, income, schooling, housing and safety.

keyPoints.memTip: Better lives on average, but the south gains most and the delta pays the price.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Use the life expectancy and infant mortality changes as evidence, and balance them with the costs.

0.question: Why is Nigeria important in its own region, West Africa?
options: It has West Africa's biggest economy and is the biggest member of ECOWAS
It is a major oil exporter, and its films are watched around the world
It has more people than any other country in the whole world
Britain once ruled it, so it now governs the other ECOWAS countries
0.correctFeedback: Right. Regional importance means mattering within West Africa. Nigeria is the region's biggest economy and the biggest member of ECOWAS.
0.wrongFeedback: Not quite. Regional importance is about West Africa. Nigeria has the region's biggest economy and is the biggest member of ECOWAS. Things known around the world show global importance instead.

1.question: How can one new factory in Lagos lead to many more jobs?
options: Workers spend their wages in local shops, which then need more staff
Factory workers leave their farms, so the farms must hire new workers
The factory trains its workers, who then each open a factory of their own
The government pays factory owners to hire more workers than they need
1.correctFeedback: Right. Wages are spent in local shops, which then hire more staff. More tax pays for schools and roads. This is the multiplier effect.
1.wrongFeedback: Not quite. Factory workers earn regular wages and spend them locally. Shops then need more staff, and the government collects more tax. This is the multiplier effect.

2.question: Which of these is a disadvantage of TNCs such as Shell for Nigeria?
options: Much of the profit goes back to the company's home country
They pay taxes to the Nigerian government
They train Nigerian workers in new skills
They build roads
2.correctFeedback: Right. When profits leave Nigeria, less of the money from oil helps Nigerians.
2.wrongFeedback: Not quite. Taxes, training and roads are advantages. Profits going back to the home country is a disadvantage.

3.question: Which of these is multilateral aid to Nigeria?
options: A United Nations project paying for clinics in Nigeria
The UK government paying for girls' schooling in Nigeria
A charity handing out mosquito nets to protect against malaria
China lending money to Nigeria to build roads and railways
3.correctFeedback: Right. Multilateral aid comes through international organisations, such as the World Bank or the United Nations.
3.wrongFeedback: Not quite. Multilateral aid comes through international organisations, such as the World Bank or the United Nations. Aid from one government to another is bilateral.

4.question: How has Nigeria's quality of life changed as its economy has developed?
options: Life expectancy has risen, but the north has gained less than the south
Life expectancy has risen, and the north and south have gained equally
Life expectancy has fallen, though more people now work in services
Infant mortality has risen as more people moved to cities
4.correctFeedback: Right. Life expectancy rose from 47 to 55 years between 2000 and 2024. But the poorer north has gained less than the south.
4.wrongFeedback: Not quite. Life expectancy has risen and infant mortality has fallen. But the poorer north has gained less than the south.

commonMistakes: Calling Nigeria an LIC. It is an NEE.
Saying oil employs most Nigerians. Oil earns most of the export money but gives few jobs, because machines do most of the work.
Saying TNCs bring jobs and money without explaining how that helps development. Explain it: wages are spent locally, and taxes pay for schools and clinics.
Writing generic answers. Use Nigeria's places: Lagos, the Niger Delta, the poorer north.
Confusing aid with TNCs, tourism or ordinary business investment. Aid is help from governments or charities: gifts, or loans on very easy terms.
Confusing Nigeria with Niger, its poorer neighbour.
examTips: For TNC questions, give an advantage and a disadvantage and explain how each affects development, using Shell or Unilever.
"Regionally important" means important within West Africa.
For development and the environment, link a gain (better jobs and health) to a cost (pollution in the Niger Delta). Give place detail.
Use evidence: life expectancy rose from 47 to 55 years between 2000 and 2024.
